AM-T650 · whole-body L1-adaptive 4-D impedance control · IsaacSim mirror of the 0918 / 0921 / 0924 flights

Sim-to-Real Flight Performance Tuning

The simulator's plant was re-identified from the three hardware campaigns and written into a new mirror configuration, …whole_body_l1_4d_direct_actuation_t650_sim.yaml, whose controller section is the hardware yaml verbatim. The former stress-test file lives on unchanged as …_sim_robustness.yaml. Below: what changed and where each number came from, then the replayed missions beside the flights they mirror, with the sim-to-real error on every state; then why DIRECT-mode mismatches remain, an audit of the arm-channel compensation against the flights, and a gain-tuning study on the circle bench that found the mechanism behind the base error and a two-gain change that halves it while still passing the robustness plant.

Four plant effects had no simulator knob before this work and were added to the Isaac plant (06) and its launcher: a yaw-coefficient scale separate from thrust, a battery-sag drift on kf, a body-fixed standing force/torque, and the Present-Velocity lag and quantum on the joint velocity the law reads; the mocap emulator gained a publish rate and measurement noise, and the servo model a per-joint friction scale.

2. Identification results per flight

Hover thrust balance from the law's own collective and the flown allocator belief; same-command test (recorded motor commands driven through the sim plant model against the measured gyro/accelerometer response, 0.3–8 Hz, coupled inertia at the folded home); observer residuals in the first hover hold; joint-velocity lag from the reported velocity against the differentiated reported position.

5. Why DIRECT-mode mismatches remain, and what was done about them

  • The clock. The dominant DIRECT-mode residual on the circle (sim CoM 94 mm vs flight 56, |e_R| 0.10 vs 0.04, a constant −5.4° yaw lag) is the wall-clock controller against an RTF 0.48 plant: the planner's reference derivatives are in wall seconds while the plant's velocities are in plant seconds, so on a yawing circle the rate feed-forward is 2× too small and the attitude loop parks at k_w·e_ω = k_R·sin(e_R) — exactly the measured lag. Running Isaac headless (RTF 0.52) already moves the CoM error to 66 mm and |e_R| to 0.066. Force and torque terms are unaffected, which is why the 0918 hold/step replays match. The real fix is a code change (controller and planner on simulated time), not a plant parameter; the offline sweep below sidesteps it by running the law at RTF 1.
  • Hover wander. The flight's 25–30 mm, 0.1 Hz CoM wander in every hold does not come from the feedback noise — with the mocap noise on, the sim hover moves 4 mm. It scales with |e_R| and the pure-P position loop, i.e. it is a slow attitude-loop mode the mirror under-excites; the gain sweep targets exactly that term.
  • Arm tracking. The sim arm follows its reference 2–4× better than hardware (stick–slip is only approximated by one tanh level per joint). Per the request, the plant was not fitted further; the compensation terms were corrected from the audit instead.
  • Model updates since the flights. The hardware yaml now carries the joint-diagonal armature with the bench values, the faster joint-velocity observer, K_y 80 / D_y 24 and the rescaled M_r_d; the mirror's section 2 was updated to match, with the as-flown values kept in comments. The replays in sections 3–4 were flown with the as-flown values (WB_REPLAY_ASFLOWN=1) so they compare like with like.
  • Inertia (X650 CAD on a T650 airframe). The mass is the weighed 3.746 kg; the inertia is inherited. The 0921 same-command test measured roll/pitch gains of 1.11 / 1.03 relative to the CAD value at the folded home, so the coupled inertia is within ~10 %; the margin sweep carries a ±25 % inertia perturbation to bound the risk.

6. Arm-channel compensation audit (0918, 0924 F1–F4)

Three compensation terms act on the streamed joint torque u3 before it reaches the servo: the gravity-scale correction (S−1)·g(q), the friction feed-forward (f_c + µ|τ|)·tanh(q̇_ref/w), and, inside the law, the observer's joint-row estimate d̂_q and the internal feed-forward. The audit compares, tick by tick, the torque the servo applied (Present Current × K_t) with the torque the chain intended, then back-solves the real kinetic friction from applied − S·g(q,R₀) − J·q̈ on the moving samples and reads the standing residual in the holds.

  • The pipeline delivers what it intends. applied − intended has a mean of ±0.01 N·m on 0918 / F3 / F4 (rms 0.06–0.14 on j2); F1/F2 show ±0.1 N·m offsets that coincide with their lower move fraction and the stick phases. The calibration (κ, S) is consistent with the flights — nothing to correct there.
  • The friction feed-forward is 30–35 % too high on j2/j3 and its structure is wrong while the joint sticks. Real kinetic level on j2 is 0.05–0.17 N·m against a 0.19–0.20 N·m feed-forward, on j3 0.00–0.09 against 0.11; pooled free fits are ill-conditioned (negative f_c with µ fixed), so the ratio is trusted, not the split. The relay fires on the reference velocity, so during a stick phase it pushes at full level while the joint is stationary, and it is exactly zero at a hold although the joint parks 1.5–3° short — the 0924 F3/F4 stick–slip signature.
  • Correction applied (hardware and Isaac arm yamls, UNFLOWN): j2 ×0.70 (0.0314 → 0.0220 N·m, µ 0.246 → 0.172), j3 ×0.65 (0.0575 → 0.0374, µ 0.161 → 0.105), and a new friction_velocity_source: measured (width 0.03 rad/s) so the relay follows the joint's own motion; j1/j4 are left alone (their residual is at the current-sensor floor). The mirror plant carries the same ratios (sim_arm_friction_scale_j2/j3 0.70/0.65). Loopback test 24/24.
  • The joint-row observer estimate is small and consistent: d̂_q on j2 +0.02…+0.08 N·m, j3 +0.01…+0.08, i.e. the residual gravity/friction error the law absorbs is under 10 % of the 0.7 N·m hold torque. The J_arm structure (now joint-diagonal with the bench values) and the faster velocity observer are in the hardware yaml and mirrored into the sim's section 2; neither was flown on 0918–0924, so the audit's numbers are the as-flown model's.
  • Not changed, on purpose: a breakaway (static) term, a gravity-integral in the pass-through (the L1 arm channel already integrates), and a velocity-dependent j4 back-EMF bias — each needs a bench measurement the flight data cannot separate.

7. Whole-body gain tuning on the circle bench

Goal. Smaller end-effector absolute error and faster full-state response on a 0.5 m radius circle at 0.13 m/s (24 s lap). On the 0924 flights the absolute EE error is the base CoM error plus a few millimetres of task error (F2: 55.9 mm EE absolute, 7.0 mm task), so the base loops are the target.

Plan. (1) Screen every gain group offline, one at a time, with the recorded 0924 F2 reference stream driving the exact Python law (the C++ port's source of truth: 4-D L1 observer, ω_x 0.25, K_y 80/24, joint-diagonal armature, rescaled M_r_d) against the mirror plant at RTF 1, the clock the hardware has. (2) Find the mechanism behind the residual so the lever is chosen, not guessed. (3) Gate every candidate on transport-delay margin, a 3 N gust, the DIRECT-entry handover and the robustness plant — the _sim_robustness stress configuration (+17.6 % kf belief, mass/inertia ×1.10, CoM 10/10/5 mm, arm ×1.05) with the tuned hardware law on it. (4) Confirm the winner in Isaac on both plants. (5) Hardware, one change per flight, repeat-tested.

The bench is sensitive to the translational observer bandwidth and the attitude/position stiffnesses, not to the EE-side gains (K_y, K_ψ, ω_x). k_x 64+ and k_R 4 already diverge against the 16 ms transport delay plus the 100 ms rotor lag, and the improvements do not stack (k_R 3 with ω_c_r 1 rings at 11° tilt).

Step 2 — the mechanism: a body-fixed force on a yawing trajectory

Ablating the mirror plant one term at a time: removing the identified body-fixed lateral force (+0.55, −0.50) N drops the circle's EE absolute error from 23.5 to 1.9 mm; removing the yaw-torque bias, the yaw-coefficient mismatch or the arm friction changes nothing. The same force fixed in the world frame costs 3.9 mm. The observer is not the problem — it estimates the force to 0.07 N rms. The problem is the law's thrust-direction rate: f_d_dot = −k_x e_v − k_v e_a + m x_cd⁽³⁾ treats d̂_t as constant, but a body-fixed force rotates in the world at the heading rate (0.26 rad/s on this circle). The commanded angular velocity ω_0c then carries a spurious 0.014 rad/s roll/pitch rate the body never has; the attitude loop parks at e_R ≈ (k_w/k_R)·e_ω = 0.014 rad (measured 0.0153), and the pure-P position loop turns that into T·e_R/k_x ≈ 18 mm. On the real 0924 F2 flight the same identity holds with |e_R| = 0.042: 36.7 × 0.042 / 32 = 48 mm against the measured 56 mm CoM error.

So the right levers are the ratio k_w/k_R and the translational observer bandwidth ω_c_t. A structural what-if — feeding the estimate's own rate into f_d_dot — recovers only 18 % and costs delay margin, so it is not pursued as a gain-tuning step.

Offline verdict. K4 (k_w 0.9 + ω_c_t 6) is the best offline: on the mirror plant it more than halves the circle error (23.5 → 10.5 mm) and the error under a 3 N gust (67.7 → 34.8 mm), rejects the gust 40 % faster (+108 mm / 2.8 s vs +183 mm / 4.3 s), cuts the entry peak 53 → 33 mm and survives a 28 ms delay where the shipped law aborts; on the robustness plant it passes every test, at the cost of a larger entry handover (539 vs 436 mm horizontal, 9.6° vs 5.6° tilt). K5 (k_R 2.5) keeps that handover but gives back the delay margin. Both K4 and k_w 0.9 alone went to Isaac.

Isaac runs at RTF ≈ 0.5 against a wall-clock law, which inflates every attitude-driven error (section on DIRECT-mode mismatches); read the Isaac rows as a relative comparison and as the pass/fail of the robustness plant, and the offline rows for the absolute size of the effect.

Isaac verdict. Both chains completed every flight, with no abort, zero rotor saturation and zero joint clamp; the shipped baseline repeats to within 2–3 mm (81.2 / 83.3 mirror, 86.1 / 86.5 robustness). k_w 0.9 alone improves BOTH plants: mirror 83.3 → 63.5 mm (−24 %), robustness 86.5 → 68.0 mm (−21 %), |e_R| 0.10 → 0.06 on both, tilt peak unchanged; its cost is the predicted larger entry handover on the robustness plant (360 → 427 mm). K4 helps the mirror less than k_w alone (69.7 mm) and makes the robustness circle worse (104 vs 86 mm, peak 185 vs 112 mm, a ringing 0.38 Hz attitude mode). Offline, doubling every observer bandwidth to emulate the wall-clock filters does not reproduce that ringing, so its source is another part of the RTF 0.49 wall-clock coupling (the observer integrates wall-clock steps over plant-time momentum changes; EKF2 runs non-lockstep) — not isolated, and not ignorable either: the robustness test is the gate the user set.

Step 5 — recommendation and hardware sequence (NOT flown)

  1. Adopt wb_k_w 1.5 → 0.9 (attitude damping ζ 1.47 → 0.88) — applied 2026-09-27, then superseded the same day by section 8's joint tune H1b, which moves k_w with every other gain group; do not revert k_w alone. The only change that improves both plants offline and in Isaac; it also adds delay margin (offline: survives 24–28 ms where 1.5 aborts) and adds no noise bandwidth. Fly hover, then the circle, twice each; score with tools/score_run.py --real.
  2. Hold wb_l1_omega_c_t at 2.0 for now. Raising it to 4–6 is the next-largest offline lever (the body-fixed force is tracked faster as it rotates), but it degraded the Isaac robustness circle and it passes more of the hardware's noisy deadbeat estimate into f_d. Re-test it once the Isaac rig runs the law on simulated time, or on hardware as a separate, repeated step after k_w with ripple watched.
  3. Structural follow-up (a law change, not a gain): the rate of the disturbance estimate is missing from f_d_dot. A body-frame translational estimate, or its rotation rate ω × d̂ fed forward, attacks the mechanism directly; the naive finite-difference what-if recovered only 18 %.

8. Circle tracking, round 2: all gain groups jointly, and the trajectory as a hyperparameter (2026-09-27)

Result. The joint tune H1b is applied to the hardware and flight-matched yamls (the robustness yaml is untouched). On the hardware-clock bench it cuts the EE absolute error by 20–32 % on every one of 48 planner-generated circles (mean −25 %); on the recommended showcase circle — r 0.75 m, 24 s lap (0.18 m/s), clockwise, arm ±15° once per lap — it goes from 20.7 to 14.1 mm. In Isaac it completes the worst-case robustness flight with 24 % less EE error than the shipped law, and flies both flight-matched circles clean. Delay margin is the shipped law's. Not flown on hardware.

The bench. circle_tune_20260927/tools/circle_bench.py flies the exact Python law (the C++ port's source of truth) against the flight-matched plant at RTF 1, on reference streams the real planner generates offline (gen_circle_stream.py, a loopback of fsc_trajectory_planner on the mirror yaml). The law sees hardware-like feedback: EKF odometry 20 ms late with band-limited velocity noise — calibrated: 2.0 cm/s reproduces the flights' hover |e_R| of 0.021 — attitude jitter, gyro noise, 12-bit encoders, and the arm observer's 12 ms lag. Every candidate sees the same noise; scoring is on the true state. It reproduces Isaac's k_w 1.5 → 0.9 gain independently.

The reference as a hyperparameter — 50 planner-generated circles

EE absolute error vs mean speed · arm ±15° once per lap · 24/28/32/40 s laps · solid = clockwise, dashed = counter-clockwise
  • The arm's motion does not matter: static, ±10° half-cycle (flown), ±10° / ±15° once per lap and ±10° twice per lap land within 0.3 mm. Showcase the ±15° lap-synced sweep for free.
  • Lap time dominates, radius barely matters: the error comes from the heading turning once per lap (section 7's mechanism), so 0.75 m costs ≤ 1 mm over 0.5 m at the same lap — 1.5× the speed for free.
  • Clockwise is 14–21 % better than counter-clockwise, and not because of the identified biases: with every bias removed the asymmetry stays (7.2 vs 8.8 mm). It is the airframe's own asymmetry (the model's Ixy, the arm's CoM offsets). All flights so far flew counter-clockwise. The body-fixed lateral force is 60 % of all the error (22.2 → 8.8 mm without it); the yaw-torque bias contributes nothing.
  • Recommended showcase: r 0.75 m, 24 s lap (0.18 m/s), clockwise, arm ±15° once per lap — planner keys ee_traj_circle_radius 0.75, ee_traj_ccw false, ee_traj_q2_amp_deg 15, ee_traj_q2_period_s 24 (the yaml defaults were left as flown).

The search: CMA-ES over 13 gains, five stages

Log-space CMA-ES (λ = 12) over k_x, k_v, k_R, k_w, an M_r_d scale, K_y, D_y, K_ψ, D_ψ, ω_c,t, ω_c,r, ω_c,q, ω_x. Each candidate flies the two performance circles plus stress runs. Cost = mean EE rms + ¼ mean EE peak, plus penalties for aborts, tilt, saturation, actuator chatter and hover quality. Every stage was stopped or redirected by something the previous one found:

  1. Circle only → 30 % better circles at k_w 0.3–0.4 (attitude ζ ≈ 0.33) that rang in hover. Hover |e_R| and CoM added to the cost.
  2. + hover quality → −35 %, but M_r_d pressed to its 0.6× bound: 1.5 mm bought with the delay margin (the 2026-08-23 lesson). The ablation below.
  3. M_r_d ≥ 0.9×, margin run at 30 ms → F3: −34 %, more delay margin than shipped. F3 then failed the Isaac robustness flight: a sustained 0.45 Hz attitude limit cycle from the moment DIRECT engaged; the circle never started.
  4. The Isaac clock, modelled. The whole-body node and its L1 observer run on the wall clock; at RTF 0.48 the predictor integrates plant-time momentum changes with the wall step, so d̂ = d − (1 − RTF)·ṗ — a positive acceleration feedback through C(s) that hardware does not have. With that in the bench (rtf=0.48: plant 0.48·dt per wall tick, reference derivatives per wall second, the arm observer's q̇ in wall units) it reproduces Isaac: shipped 104.7 vs 106.4 mm, F3 81.5 vs 80.9 mm, |e_R| 0.071/0.088 vs 0.069/0.088, and F3's robustness failure. The Isaac robustness run became a fifth gate.
  5. The consistent bar — no worse than shipped on every gate (28 ms delay; the Isaac robustness run completes with hover, entry, circle error and tilt within 10 % of shipped and |e_R| bounded) → H1. H1 then failed the flight-matched plant in Isaac: its stiffer arm task (K_y 270, ω_c,q 1.10, ω_x 0.28) oscillated joints 2/3 at ~2.5 Hz onto the 3 N·m clamp once the circle started. The bench could not reproduce this — not with Isaac's 0.020 plant armature, the friction relay on Present Velocity, nor 24 ms of arm-command delay — so where the bench is blind the arm side was taken from F3, which Isaac had already flown clean: H1b. The arm group is worth only ±0.4 mm on the bench.

Two sim findings worth acting on. (1) The flight-matched yaml was meant to carry the bench-calibrated arm armature (sim_arm_armature_j1..j4, the law's own [0.010, 0.0194, 0.0097, 0.0097]) and does not, so every Isaac mirror flight has had PhysX's 0.020 on every joint; the bench says it barely matters, but the mirror should carry it. (2) The Isaac robustness failures of stronger tunes (K4 on 09-26, F3 here) are the wall-clock observer artefact above; running the whole-body node and planner on simulated time would remove it and let Isaac test what hardware will fly.

9. What the mirror still cannot reproduce

  • Real-time factor. Isaac and PX4 run at RTF ≈ 0.5 on this desktop while the law (250 Hz) and planner (100 Hz) run on the wall clock. Force and torque terms are time-invariant, but every filter — the L1 C(s), ω_x, the joint-row trim — is about twice as fast in plant time. The replays scale the planner's kinematic bounds and the EE-trajectory time scale by RTF so the plant sees the flown pace; nothing else can be corrected without running the controller in simulated time.
  • Feedback noise. The emulated mocap is the exact PhysX state at 250 Hz; the real feeds carried 1.2–2.9 cm/s of hover velocity noise (fused / raw 60 Hz) and 10 cm/s at raw 120 Hz. The sim's actuator ripple is correspondingly lower.
  • Friction shape. One tanh level per joint, no separate breakaway; the hardware arm's stick–slip bursts (0924 F3/F4) are only approximated.
  • Yaw asymmetry is a constant body torque, not a per-rotor drag difference; battery sag is linear in time, not a function of current draw.

10. Reproduce

  • docs/docs_aerial_manipulator/sim2real_tuning_20260926/tools/extract_all.sh — the six bags → npz.
  • /usr/bin/python3 tools/fit_plant.py data — identification (analysis/fit_plant.{json,txt}).
  • tools/replay.sh f18|a2|a3 <tag> — one Isaac replay on the mirror plant (records a bag, restores the yaml).
  • tools/compare.py data/<flight>.npz data/sim_<tag>.npz <tag> then tools/build_report.py.
  • Profiles: WB_SIM_PROFILE=mirror (default) or robustness on both the stack script and the Pegasus launcher.
  • /usr/bin/python3 tools/arm_comp_audit.py — the arm-channel compensation audit (analysis/arm_comp_audit.{json,txt}).
  • /usr/bin/python3 tools/circle_sweep.py --baseline|--sweep|--combo|--gate — the offline circle bench (exact law, mirror or robustness plant, profile=); gust/entry/delay metrics in simulate().
  • circle_tune_20260927/tools/: gen_circle_stream.py / gen_grid.py (planner reference streams, offline), circle_bench.py (the bench; rtf=0.48 = the Isaac clock), tune_cma.py (the search), final_gate.py, eval_grid.py, gains_to_yaml.py (bench names → yaml keys, --apply), run_isaac_set.sh (Isaac flights from a spec file).
  • tools/run_gain_isaac.sh "wb_k_w=0.9,wb_l1_omega_c_t=6.0" — the four Isaac confirmation flights (replay.sh with WB_REPLAY_PROFILE / WB_REPLAY_GAINS), scored by tools/score_run.py.
